sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Niraparib was approved in the EU in 2017 as maintenance treatment for platinum-sensitive, recurrent ovarian cancer, and in 2020 as first-line maintenance after response to platinum-based chemotherapy. Results from a prospective, noninterventional, single-arm, postauthorization safety study characterizing the risk of developing myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS)/acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and other second primary malignancies (SPMs) in patients treated with niraparib in routine clinical practice are reported.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: Adult patients with epithelial ovarian cancer from Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, and Spain who received niraparib maintenance were enrolled. Patients were followed from niraparib initiation (index date) to the earliest of study completion at 5 years’ follow-up, study discontinuation, death, or final database lock (July 11, 2024). Incidence of MDS/AML, and other SPMs were reported, and treatment-emergent adverse events were summarized. Analyses were stratified by niraparib maintenance treatment line.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Overall, 745 patients (181 first-line maintenance; 564 recurrent) were enrolled and included in this analysis (median age, 65 years; stage III/IV at diagnosis, 89.5%; high-grade serous ovarian cancer at enrollment, 98.7%). Among patients tested for BRCA (n = 585), 14.7% had BRCA-mutated status. Median (Q1, Q3) niraparib treatment duration was 11.0 (5.1, 20.0) and 10.4 (4.8, 22.9) months in first-line maintenance and recurrent cohorts, respectively. Nine patients (1.2%) experienced 11 MDS/AML events, with an incidence rate of 0.51 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.23–0.97) per 100 patient-years. Six patients (0.8%) experienced seven SPMs, with an incidence rate of 0.34 (95% CI 0.12–0.74) per 100 patient-years. All events occurred in the recurrent cohort, except one SPM event in the first-line cohort.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Results were consistent with the known niraparib safety profile. For all safety outcomes, observed event rates were consistent with those reported in the label and in niraparib clinical trials. No new safety signals were observed.

tr.td: In patients with advanced ovarian cancer, treatment with platinum-based chemotherapy and maintenance therapy with poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitors have been shown to be associated with an increased risk for myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS)/acute myeloid leukemia (AML) in clinical trials and retrospective real-world analyses.

This prospective real-world study with up to 5 years of follow-up evaluated the incidence of MDS/AML and other second primary malignancies in patients with ovarian cancer treated with niraparib maintenance in routine clinical practice in the first-line and recurrent settings.

bold.italic: What was learned from this study?

tr.td: Real-world findings reinforce the niraparib safety profile observed in clinical trials.

Consistent with clinical expectations, all MDS/AML events occurred in patients who received multiple lines of platinum-based chemotherapy and were treated with niraparib maintenance therapy in the recurrent setting.
Results can be used to inform treatment decisions for patients in clinical practice with advanced ovarian cancer eligible to receive niraparib maintenance therapy.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: In patients with primary advanced or recurrent ovarian cancer that is sensitive to platinum-based chemotherapy, maintenance therapy with poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitors may be recommended to help extend progression-free survival [1, 2]. The PARP inhibitor niraparib was approved in the European Union (EU) in 2017 as maintenance treatment for platinum-sensitive, recurrent (second-line maintenance and later) ovarian cancer, and in 2020 as first-line maintenance after a response to platinum-based chemotherapy [3, 4]. These approvals were based on findings from the phase 3 double-blind placebo-controlled ENGOT-OV16/NOVA and PRIMA/ENGOT-OV26/GOG-3012 trials that demonstrated significantly improved progression-free survival with niraparib maintenance therapy compared with placebo [5, 6].

Similar to other forms of cancer, patients with ovarian cancer are inherently at an increased risk for secondary malignancies [7]. Multiple contributing factors have been identified, including genetic predisposition, lifestyle, and environmental factors associated with the initial cancer diagnosis as well as cancer treatments, such as radiation and platinum-based chemotherapy [7–9]. One of the most common second primary malignancies (SPMs) is myelodysplastic syndrome/acute myeloid leukemia (MDS/AML) [9]. PARP inhibitor treatment has been associated with an increased risk of MDS/AML [10–12]. Similar to platinum-based chemotherapy, PARP inhibitors also result in DNA damage, which has been associated with therapy-related myeloid cancers [9, 10]. Duration of treatment also matters, with an increased risk for MDS/AML observed with a longer period of treatment for platinum-based chemotherapy [13, 14]. Interestingly, data have indicated no clear association between PARP inhibitor use and SPMs outside of MDS/AML [15].

Genetic and environmental risk factors can also contribute to the development of secondary MDS/AML [9]. Consistent with the role of BRCA genes in DNA repair, patients with BRCA1/2 mutations have been shown to be at an increased risk of therapy-related MDS/AML [9]. Accordingly, understanding the contribution of PARP inhibitors to therapy-related MDS/AML and SPMs within the ovarian cancer treatment landscape is complex.

This postauthorization safety study was conducted to estimate the incidence of MDS/AML and other SPMs in patients with ovarian cancer who were treated with niraparib in routine clinical practice in Europe (ENCEPP registration number, EUPAS29407).

sec.title: Study Design, Setting, and Patient Population
sec.p: Patients were enrolled into this prospective noninterventional single-arm study from sites in the European countries of Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, and Spain, all of which had niraparib maintenance therapy approved for use in ovarian cancer in the second-line or later (recurrent), and, subsequently, first-line maintenance settings (Supplementary Material Table 1). Study sites were eligible for inclusion in this study if niraparib was being used in accordance with the EU Summary of Product Characteristics guidelines [16]. Sites participating in the niraparib European Expanded Access Program were permitted. Enrollment began on November 6, 2019, for patients in the recurrent setting; on December 7, 2020, enrollment was opened for patients who received niraparib in the first-line maintenance setting. Enrollment for both cohorts closed on January 17, 2023, and database lock was reached on July 11, 2024.

The study included female patients aged ≥18 years with advanced epithelial ovarian, fallopian tube, or primary peritoneal cancer (collectively referred to as ovarian cancer) who received niraparib maintenance therapy. Eligible patients who received niraparib in the first-line maintenance setting had advanced epithelial (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics stage III or IV) high-grade ovarian cancer that was in complete or partial response to first-line platinum-based chemotherapy. Eligible patients who received niraparib in the recurrent setting had platinum-sensitive relapsed high-grade serous epithelial ovarian cancer that was in a complete or partial response to platinum-based chemotherapy. Patients who initiated niraparib before the time of enrollment were eligible. Patients were excluded if they received niraparib for a nonapproved use, as part of a GSK-sponsored clinical trial in which they were still participating in active follow-up, or as part of a GSK-supported study.

This study was conducted in accordance with the ethical principles founded in the Declaration of Helsinki. Before study conduct, all study documentation was reviewed and approved by an institutional review board and independent ethics committee to safeguard the rights, safety, and well-being of patients. All patients completed a written informed consent form before enrollment, according to the regulatory and legal requirements of the participating country.

sec.title: Study Conduct and Data Collection
sec.p: Patients were followed from the index date, defined as niraparib treatment initiation, to the earliest of 5 years of follow-up (study completion), lost to follow-up, study discontinuation, death, or final database lock (July 11, 2024). Specific reasons for discontinuation included withdrawal of consent, loss to follow-up, death from any cause, or sponsor decision to terminate the study. Patients were considered lost to follow-up if they missed three expected visits and did not respond to three attempts (one via certified mail) to determine the reason for study discontinuation.

Data were collected from electronic health records using electronic case report forms developed for this study. Data collection started at the time of enrollment and continued quarterly for the duration of study enrollment.

Baseline data, including patient demographics, were collected relative to the date of study enrollment or index date. Characteristics collected relative to the study enrollment date included, but were not limited to, family cancer history, smoking history, and alcohol use, and genetic assessments of BRCA/homologous recombination deficiency. The type of cytoreductive surgery was not reported systematically across sites and, therefore, was derived based on timing of surgery and first-line therapy initiation. Data on treatment, study outcomes, and other adverse events (AEs) were collected during the follow-up period (up to 5 years). All follow-up data were collected prospectively, except for patients who initiated niraparib before enrollment, for whom some data, including MDS/AML and SPM events, were collected retrospectively.

MDS/AML and other SPM data were collected and reported from first dose of niraparib until death or until the patient was lost to follow-up, whichever occurred first. All other AEs were collected and recorded for each patient during the treatment-emergent period, defined as the time from the signing of the informed consent form through 30 days after the last dose of niraparib or the patient’s death from any cause, whichever occurred first. For patients who initiated niraparib before enrollment, MDS/AML and other SPM data were collected and reported from first dose of niraparib; all other AE data were not captured retrospectively. If there was reasonable belief that a serious AE that occurred after the 30-day window was related to study drug, it was also reported to the safety database for inclusion within the study. Concomitant illnesses present before enrollment were not considered AEs unless the illness worsened during the treatment period. All AEs were coded by system organ class and preferred term per the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities version 27.0, and graded using the National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 5.0. An adverse event was assumed to be treatment-emergent if it could not be definitively shown that the AE did not occur or worsen during the treatment-emergent period.

sec.title: Outcomes of Interest
sec.p: The primary objective of this study was to estimate the incidence rates of MDS/AML and other SPMs per 100 person-time units in the overall population and in first-line maintenance and recurrent cohorts. The number of MDS/AML and/or other SPM events across known risk factors such as age, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy, and BRCA/homologous recombination deficiency status was also examined. Other AEs were summarized.

sec.title: Statistical Analysis Methods
sec.p: Study size and duration were based on data from the ENGOT-OV16/NOVA clinical trial with considerations for the required length of follow-up and the high risk of missing data and loss to follow-up in a noninterventional, real-world study. The planned sample size for this study was up to 800 patients for 1000 patient-years collected over a maximum of 5 years of follow-up per patient. Analyses were performed in the safety population, defined as all patients who were enrolled, met eligibility criteria, received ≥ 1 dose of niraparib, and had sufficient clinical information to identify their niraparib line of therapy. Analyses were descriptive, with summary statistics reported for all outcomes. No hypotheses were tested.

Analyses were conducted in the overall population and with patients grouped into two cohorts according to whether they received niraparib maintenance therapy in the first-line or recurrent setting (second-line maintenance or later). Line of therapy was derived from ovarian cancer therapies, using therapy start dates, therapy end dates, and line of therapy type (maintenance treatment, response to nonmaintenance treatment, and line of therapy assignment where available). Outliers in each cohort were reviewed by a board-certified gynecologic oncologist to confirm appropriate cohort assignment.

Patient-years were measured from index to the earliest onset date of event of interest or to the earliest occurrence of date of study discontinuation, death, or final database lock for patients who did not develop an event. Incidence rates and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) per 100 patient-years for MDS/AML and SPMs were estimated overall and among first-line maintenance and recurrent cohorts. The incidence rate of MDS/AML was measured from index to the earliest onset date of MDS or AML; the incidence rate of SPMs was measured from index to the earliest onset date of SPMs, not including MDS or AML. Time to onset of MDS/AML and other SPMs was also calculated. If a patient experienced the same treatment-emergent AE (TEAE) more than once with a different severity grade, the event with the highest grade was considered for data summaries by intensity.

Incomplete dates related to MDS/AML and other SPM outcomes were not imputed. Incomplete niraparib treatment, other treatments, AE start, and ovarian cancer diagnosis dates were imputed where possible; other variables with missing values were categorized as missing or unknown. All analyses were performed using SAS version 9.4 or later.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: In total, 745 patients were included in the safety population after all inclusion and exclusion criteria were applied, with 181 (24.3%) and 564 (75.7%) patients in the first-line maintenance and recurrent cohorts, respectively (Fig. 1). Most patients (72.9%) had niraparib exposure before study enrollment (first-line maintenance, 112 patients; recurrent, 431 patients). In the overall safety population, the median age at index was 65 years (IQR, 58–72), 66.8% of patients had stage III disease at diagnosis, and 98.7% had high-grade serous histology (Table 1). BRCA test results were available for 78.5% of patients overall. In the first-line maintenance cohort, 88.5% (108 of 122) of patients with BRCA status test results had BRCA wild-type (BRCAwt) status, and 10.7% (13 of 122) had BRCA-mutated (BRCAm) status. In the recurrent cohort, 83.8% (388 of 463) of patients with BRCA status test results had BRCAwt status, and 15.8% (73 of 463) had BRCAm status. The median time from ovarian cancer diagnosis to the start of niraparib treatment was 7.4 months (IQR, 6.7–8.6 months) for patients in the first-line maintenance cohort and 36.3 months (27.2–55.1 months) for patients in the recurrent cohort.

sec.p: In the first-line maintenance cohort, 152 patients (84.0%) and 65 patients (35.9%) completed 1 and 2 years of follow-up, respectively (Supplementary Material Table 2). In the recurrent cohort, 486 (86.2%) patients and 335 (59.4%) patients completed 1 and 2 years of follow-up, respectively (Supplementary Material Table 2). At the time of database lock, a total of 1762.6 patient-years were accumulated to the first of any event (322.9 patient-years in the first-line cohort and 1439.6 patient-years in the recurrent cohort).

The median duration of niraparib treatment was 10.7 months (IQR, 4.8–21.1 months) in the overall population, 11.0 months (IQR, 5.1–20.0 months) in the first-line maintenance cohort, and 10.4 months (4.8–22.9 months) in the recurrent cohort. The starting dose of niraparib was most commonly 200 mg for both study cohorts (first-line maintenance, 78.5%; recurrent, 62.2%; Table 2). Approximately one-half of patients in the first-line maintenance (52.5%) and recurrent (49.8%) cohorts had ≥ 1 dose modification. Dose interruptions occurred for 89 patients (49.2%) and 243 patients (43.1%) in the first-line maintenance and recurrent cohorts, respectively. Thrombocytopenia followed by anemia were the most frequent reasons for both dose modifications and dose interruptions across cohorts. Other reasons for dose modifications and interruptions included other AEs, patient request, and physician decision. In both cohorts, the most common reason for treatment discontinuation was disease progression.

sec.p: Nine patients (1.2%) experienced 11 MDS/AML events over 1767.6 patient-years, corresponding to an incidence rate of 0.51 (95% CI 0.23–0.97) per 100 patient-years (Table 3). All MDS/AML events occurred in the recurrent cohort, with an incidence rate of 0.62 (95% CI 0.29–1.18) per 100 patient-years. Two patients had both MDS and AML events. The median time from niraparib initiation to MDS/AML event onset was 32.7 months (IQR, 22.6–36.3 months). Of the nine patients who developed MDS/AML, seven had BRCAwt biomarker status (of 388 patients with BRCAwt disease in the recurrent cohort), and two had BRCAm biomarker status (of 73 patients with BRCAm disease in the recurrent cohort). All nine patients had received platinum-based chemotherapy before niraparib initiation, with a median of 14 cycles (IQR, 12–20 cycles).

sec.p: A total of seven SPMs other than MDS/AML were experienced by six patients (0.8%) in total, corresponding to an incidence rate of 0.34 (95% CI 0.12–0.74) per 100 patient-years (Table 3). Of these six patients, five were in the recurrent cohort, and one was in the first-line maintenance cohort. SPMs were breast cancer (two patients), basal cell carcinoma (two events in one patient), chronic myeloid leukemia, head and neck cancer, and squamous cell carcinoma of the oral cavity. Overall, the median time from niraparib initiation to event onset was 15.4 months (IQR, 9.5–32.1 months). One patient with a second primary malignancy had BRCAm status. All six patients with SPMs had received platinum-based chemotherapy before niraparib initiation, with a median of 12 cycles (IQR, 10–12 cycles).

Details on TEAEs are presented in Table 4. Briefly, 52.2% of patients in the overall population experienced ≥1 TEAE: 110 patients (60.8%) in the first-line maintenance cohort and 279 (49.5%) in the recurrent cohort. Overall, 18.5% of patients experienced ≥1 grade 3 or higher TEAEs. Frequency of grade ≥3 TEAEs was similar across cohorts and occurred in 36 patients (19.9%) in the first-line maintenance cohort and 102 patients (18.1%) in the recurrent cohort. There were no fatal TEAEs in the first-line maintenance cohort. Three fatal TEAEs occurred in the recurrent cohort (one event each of ascites due to disease progression, AML, and cerebral infarction); of these, only the event of AML was reported as related to niraparib per the investigator.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this prospective noninterventional single-arm postauthorization safety study of 745 patients, with more than 1760 patient-years of follow-up accumulated, the overall incidence rates for MDS/AML and SPMs were 0.51 (95% CI 0.23–0.97) and 0.34 (95% CI 0.12–0.74) per 100 patient-years, respectively. All events of MDS/AML and five of six patients who experienced events of other SPMs occurred in the recurrent cohort. Grade ≥3 TEAEs occurred in approximately 20% of patients in both the first-line maintenance and recurrent cohorts. One fatal TEAE that was investigator-assessed to be related to niraparib was reported (AML). No new safety signals were identified.

These results are generally consistent with the incidence of MDS/AML reported in the pivotal trials for niraparib maintenance therapy in ovarian cancer. In the NOVA trial of niraparib maintenance therapy in the recurrent setting, the overall incidence of MDS/AML was 3.8% in patients receiving niraparib versus 1.7% in patients receiving placebo with a median follow-up of 6.3 years [17]. In the niraparib arm, most patients (10 of 14) with MDS/AML events had germline BRCAm disease. Eight patients had received ≥ 3 lines of platinum-based therapy before initiating niraparib treatment within NOVA, and eight patients received additional subsequent anticancer therapy, including two patients who went on to receive additional PARP inhibitor treatment [17]. In the PRIMA trial of niraparib maintenance in the first-line setting, the overall incidence of MDS/AML was 2.3% in the niraparib arm and 1.6% in the placebo arm, with a median follow-up of 6.2 years [18]. In the niraparib arm, 6 of the 11 patients with MDS/AML events had BRCAm disease; 3 patients also went on to receive subsequent platinum-based chemotherapy, including 1 patient who also received a PARP inhibitor during follow-up [18].

Although direct comparisons between real-world and clinical trial data are not reliable because of inherent differences in study setting and conduct, findings from this study reinforce safety results from the PRIMA and NOVA trials. Consistent with the rigors of monitoring and reporting in clinical trials, the percentages of patients reporting any-grade, grade ≥ 3, and serious TEAEs were higher in NOVA and PRIMA than reported in this real-world observational study [6, 18]. In this study, AE data were not retrospectively collected for patients who initiated niraparib treatment before enrollment, which may have also contributed to lower TEAE rates in this study. However, it is also possible that TEAE rates were truly lower in the real-world, potentially because of the introduction of the individualized starting dose in the first-line setting, which was shown to reduce the overall incidence of grade ≥ 3 TEAEs in PRIMA [18, 19], or through improved clinician education on management of toxicities associated with niraparib [20]. Importantly, all TEAEs reported within this postauthorization safety study aligned with previous findings and the established safety profile of niraparib.

Strengths of this study include its real-world prospective design, large patient population, and extended follow-up, with more than 1700 patient-years accumulated to assess MDS/AML and SPM risk in patients treated with niraparib in routine clinical practice. Several key limitations should be considered when interpreting these findings. First, line of therapy (first-line maintenance and second-line and later maintenance) was not directly captured with the expansion of the study to include patients who received niraparib first-line maintenance. Therefore, this information had to be derived retrospectively, which may have contributed to line-of-therapy misclassification. Eight patients were excluded from the study because of insufficient clinical information to classify niraparib use in the first-line or recurrent setting. The delayed expansion of the study to include niraparib first-line maintenance patients contributed to limited follow-up time in these patients. Additionally, 72.9% of patients initiated niraparib before the time of enrollment. For these patients, some follow-up data were collected retrospectively, which may have introduced information bias. However, sensitivity analysis of baseline characteristics and treatments stratified by timing of niraparib initiation were generally similar. Additionally, some patients terminated niraparib treatment before enrollment but were still considered eligible. Immortal time bias may also have been introduced for safety events other than MDS/AML and other SPMs because AE data were not captured retrospectively for patients who initiated niraparib before enrollment; accordingly, these patients contributed person-time but not safety events to the analysis.

These results offer patients and providers important, real-world insights into the risk of MDS/AML with niraparib use. In this study, patients who developed MDS/AML also had established risk factors for these events, such as exposure to platinum-based chemotherapy and BRCAm disease, indicating providers should be cognizant of this increased risk when prescribing niraparib to patients with known risk factors. Consistent with clinical expectation, results also suggest that MDS/AML events occurred primarily in previously treated patients with recurrent disease.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Study results were consistent with the known niraparib safety profile. For all safety outcomes, including MDS/AML and SPMs, the observed incidence was consistent with those reported in the label and in niraparib clinical trials. No new safety signals were observed.

sec.title: Ethical Approval
sec.p: This study was conducted in accordance with the ethical principles founded in the Declaration of Helsinki. Before study conduct, all study documentation was reviewed and approved by an institutional review board and independent ethics committee to safeguard the rights, safety, and well-being of patients. All patients completed a written informed consent form before enrollment, according to the regulatory and legal requirements of the participating country.
